QuestionText: Photosynthesis uses sunlight CO2 and water to make glucose and O2
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

QuestionText: Raw materials for photosynthesis are CO2 and water
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: CO2 and water are the inorganic reactants for photosynthesis.

QuestionText: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that traps sunlight for photosynthesis
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

QuestionText: Chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Chloroplasts are the organelles containing chlorophyll.

QuestionText: O2 is released as a by-product of photosynthesis
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: O2 comes from splitting of water molecules in the light reactions.

QuestionText: Cuscuta has no chlorophyll and is a parasitic plant
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Cuscuta wraps around host plants and absorbs nutrients directly.

QuestionText: Pitcher plant is insectivorous and obtains nitrogen from insects
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Pitcher plant traps insects for nitrogen in N-poor soils.

QuestionText: Rhizobium bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen in root nodules of legumes
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Rhizobium converts N2 into ammonia usable by plants.

QuestionText: Autotrophic organisms make their own food from inorganic substances
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Autotrophs (green plants) produce organic food from CO2 and H2O.

QuestionText: Heterotrophic organisms obtain food by consuming others
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Heterotrophs (animals) cannot make their own food.

QuestionText: Saprophytes break down dead organic matter for nutrition
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Saprophytes (fungi, bacteria) decompose dead matter and absorb nutrients.

QuestionText: Starch in leaves is tested with iodine solution (blue-black colour)
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Iodine → blue-black indicates starch (photosynthesis product).

QuestionText: Variegated leaf experiment proves chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Only green (chlorophyll) regions turn blue-black with iodine.

QuestionText: KOH experiment proves CO2 is needed for photosynthesis
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: KOH removes CO2; leaves without CO2 show no starch.

QuestionText: Covering part of leaf with black paper proves light is needed
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Covered region (no light) shows no starch; uncovered region shows starch.

QuestionText: Xylem transports water and minerals from roots to leaves
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Xylem: unidirectional flow of water and mineral salts upward.

QuestionText: Phloem transports food (sucrose) from leaves to all plant parts
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Phloem: bidirectional transport of organic solutes.

QuestionText: Stomata are pores on leaves for gas exchange
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: CO2 enters and O2/H2O vapour exit through stomata.

QuestionText: Guard cells control opening and closing of stomata
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Guard cell turgor pressure changes open/close stomata.

QuestionText: In the dark plants only respire and do not photosynthesize
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Photosynthesis requires light; respiration is continuous.

QuestionText: Herbivores eat only plants
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Herbivores (cow, rabbit, deer) feed exclusively on plants.

QuestionText: Carnivores eat only other animals
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Carnivores (lion, eagle) feed exclusively on animals.

QuestionText: Omnivores eat both plants and animals
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Omnivores (humans, bears) eat both plant and animal food.

QuestionText: The primary energy source for life on Earth is sunlight via photosynthesis
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Almost all ecosystem energy derives from solar energy captured by photosynthesis.

QuestionText: A food chain always starts with a producer (green plant)
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Producers capture solar energy: base of all food chains.

QuestionText: Decomposers recycle nutrients by breaking down dead organisms
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Bacteria and fungi break down dead matter into inorganic compounds.

QuestionText: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour mainly through leaf stomata
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Transpiration stream drives water up through xylem.

QuestionText: Light intensity is a limiting factor for photosynthesis
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Increasing light boosts photosynthesis rate up to saturation point.

QuestionText: Magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Mg2+ is at the centre of chlorophyll's porphyrin ring.

QuestionText: Nitrogen deficiency causes yellowing (chlorosis) in plants
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Nitrogen is needed for chlorophyll; deficiency causes chlorosis.

QuestionText: Chemosynthesis uses chemical energy (not light) to make food
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Chemoautotrophs oxidise inorganic compounds for energy.

QuestionText: Aquatic plants often have stomata on upper leaf surface
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Upper surface stomata allow gas exchange with atmosphere above water.

QuestionText: Palisade mesophyll cells are densely packed with chloroplasts
Options: C) Spongy mesophyll is main site
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Palisade cells near upper leaf surface: primary photosynthesis site.

QuestionText: Glucose formula is C6H12O6 with C:H:O ratio of 1:2:1
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: 6C:12H:6O simplifies to 1:2:1.

QuestionText: Transpiration pull drives water up xylem by cohesion-tension mechanism
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Transpiration creates tension; cohesion of water molecules transmits this up xylem.

QuestionText: Aerobic respiration: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely.

QuestionText: Plants respire 24 hours a day (day and night)
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Respiration is continuous in all living cells.

QuestionText: Phosphorus is essential for root development and ATP (energy transfer)
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Phosphorus is part of ATP and DNA; essential for roots and flowering.

QuestionText: Potassium regulates stomatal opening via guard cell turgor
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: K+ ions enter guard cells; water follows by osmosis; stomata open.

QuestionText: Carnivorous plants get nitrogen from insects they capture
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: In N-poor soil carnivorous plants supplement nitrogen by digesting insects.

QuestionText: White regions of variegated leaf cannot photosynthesize (no chlorophyll)
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: No chlorophyll = no photosynthesis regardless of light availability.

QuestionText: Root hair cells use active transport to absorb minerals against concentration gradient
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Active transport uses energy (ATP) to move minerals into root cells.

QuestionText: Algae produce roughly half of Earth's oxygen
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Marine phytoplankton account for ~50% of global photosynthesis.

QuestionText: Calcium is essential for strong bones and teeth in animals
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Calcium (Ca) is the main mineral in bone and tooth structures.

QuestionText: Iodine solution turns blue-black in presence of starch
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Classic test for starch: iodine turns from yellow-brown to blue-black.

QuestionText: Fungi obtain nutrition by absorbing from dead or living organic matter
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Fungi are heterotrophic absorbers (saprophytic or parasitic).

QuestionText: The word for plants making their own food is autotrophic nutrition
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Auto = self; autotrophic plants produce their own organic food.

QuestionText: The word equation for photosynthesis: CO2 + H2O + light → glucose + O2
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: This is the standard word equation for photosynthesis.

QuestionText: Assimilation is the process by which cells use absorbed nutrients
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Assimilation: absorbed nutrients are used to build cell components and release energy.

QuestionText: Nitrogen in soil comes partly from bacterial decomposition and nitrogen fixation
Topic: Chemistry/Biology - Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Explanation: Nitrogen enters soil through decomposition of organic matter and biological nitrogen fixation.
